intro: The purpose of Becoming Like Jesus is to help us come more fully unto Jesus Christ, become more like Him, and help others come unto Him.
instructions: Do not answer according to what you believe, intend to do, or think a disciple should do. Think about specific experiences from the requested time period and answer according to what you actually thought, desired, said, and did. When possible, recall at least three recent examples. If responses varied, score the pattern rather than your best or worst moment.
disclaimer: This assessment is a tool for honest reflection, not an authoritative or complete measurement of discipleship, righteousness, worthiness, spiritual standing, or our relationship with God. Becoming Like Jesus is an independent, noncommercial personal discipleship project. It is not an official publication of, nor is it sponsored, endorsed, or approved by, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
outro: Now Set the Score Aside
The purpose of this assessment was never simply to produce a number.
Its purpose is to help you remember, examine, and become.

These questions are intended to remind us of many of the attributes, teachings, patterns, practices, and covenant responsibilities associated with following Jesus Christ - and to help us consider how they are actually appearing in the ordinary circumstances of our lives. Periodically returning to these questions may help us recognize patterns we have stopped noticing, remember principles we have neglected, see opportunities to change, and become more intentional about becoming like the Savior.

This assessment is not intended to replace prayer, scripture study, worship, listening to living prophets and Apostles, receiving personal revelation, or any other part of discipleship. Those are indispensable. Rather, it can serve somewhat like periodically reading a thoughtful gospel-centered book: it can gather scriptural principles into one place, remind us of things we already know, invite us to see familiar truths in new ways, and help us consider their practical application in everyday life on the covenant path.

The score can be useful - but only as a tool. It may help identify an area that deserves greater attention, reveal a pattern that is changing, or help us recognize growth over time. But the number itself is not the objective.
Ultimately, this assessment invites us to consider a much deeper question:
WHO AM I BECOMING?

One day each of us will stand before Jesus Christ and account for our lives. We should not presume to know precisely what questions He will ask or how He will judge us. But scripture teaches that our choices matter not only because of what we do, but because of what those choices help us become.
So look at your score long enough to learn from it. Then set it aside. Turn again toward Jesus Christ.
What am I still holding back from Jesus Christ?
Lord, what lack I yet?
What am I not seeing?
What would Thou have me change?
What would Thou have me begin doing - or stop doing?
Whom would Thou have me love, forgive, serve, help, or reconcile with?
What would Thou have me give, surrender, repair, or become?
Then listen for the Holy Ghost. And when the Lord helps you recognize something, act.
"Come unto Christ, and be perfected in him." - Moroni 10:32
Look inward long enough to see honestly. Then look upward to Christ and move forward.
The scorecard is not the destination. Jesus Christ is.

categories.title: Faith in & Devotion to Jesus Christ / Relationship with the Godhead

questions.title: Do I exercise faith in Jesus Christ as my Savior and Redeemer?
questions.prompt: During the past seven days, how consistently did I consciously place faith in Jesus Christ - relying on Him, His promises, His grace, and His redeeming power rather than merely believing facts about Him?
questions.christ_example: Christ repeatedly invited people to believe in Him and act in faith (Mark 5:34-36; John 11:25-27).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where did my choices this week reveal actual reliance on Christ?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.1 - Do I exercise faith in Jesus Christ as my Savior and Redeemer?"

anchors.1: Faith in Christ rarely enters how I actually face life; I mostly rely on myself or other sources.
anchors.4: I sometimes consciously rely on Christ, especially in obvious spiritual needs, but it is inconsistent.
anchors.7: Conscious reliance on Jesus Christ is increasingly characteristic of my daily life; I trust Him and act because I trust Him.

questions.title: Do I apply the Atonement of Jesus Christ to my actual life?
questions.prompt: During the past seven days, how intentionally did I turn to Jesus Christ and His Atonement for forgiveness, strength, healing, understanding, succor, change, and power beyond my own?
questions.christ_example: In Gethsemane and on the cross, Jesus Christ took upon Himself sin, pain, infirmity, and death (Luke 22:39-44; John 19).
questions.reflection_prompt: What burden am I carrying as though Christ cannot help me with it?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.2 - Do I apply the Atonement of Jesus Christ to my actual life?"

anchors.1: I rarely think of the Atonement as relevant to my present struggles beyond a general belief in it.
anchors.4: I sometimes turn to Christ for forgiveness or strength, but often try to carry burdens alone.
anchors.7: Turning to Christ's Atonement for forgiveness, succor, strength, healing, and transformation is increasingly a lived pattern.

questions.title: Do I turn toward Christ when I am afraid, uncertain, or overwhelmed?
questions.prompt: Think of recent moments of fear, uncertainty, stress, or discouragement. How consistently did I turn toward Jesus Christ in faith rather than allowing fear alone to direct my thinking and choices?
questions.christ_example: During the storm, Christ asked His disciples why they were fearful and invited faith (Mark 4:37-40).
questions.reflection_prompt: What would trusting Christ change about the way I am facing my present uncertainty?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.3 - Do I turn toward Christ when I am afraid, uncertain, or overwhelmed?"

anchors.1: Fear or uncertainty usually drives my reactions, with little conscious turning to Christ.
anchors.4: I sometimes pray or remember Christ, but anxiety often continues to control my choices.
anchors.7: I increasingly bring fear and uncertainty to Christ, seek His guidance, and move forward in faith even before circumstances are resolved.

questions.title: Do I trust God when His plan differs from mine?
questions.prompt: When outcomes, timing, or answers differ from what I want, how consistently do I continue trusting Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ rather than withdrawing, demanding my preferred outcome, or assuming I know better?
questions.christ_example: Jesus Christ submitted perfectly to the Father's will in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where am I asking God to approve my plan rather than sincerely seeking His?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.4 - Do I trust God when His plan differs from mine?"

anchors.1: I tend to resist God when His apparent answer conflicts with what I want.
anchors.4: I accept some disappointments faithfully but struggle to trust when the issue matters deeply to me.
anchors.7: Trusting God's wisdom is increasingly characteristic; I seek His will, act faithfully, and entrust outcomes to Him even when they differ from my hopes.

questions.title: Is Jesus Christ increasingly the center of how I understand and live my life?
questions.prompt: During ordinary life - not only during prayer, scripture study, worship, or crisis - how consistently do I consciously look to Jesus Christ and His Atonement as the center of my perspective, decisions, hopes, identity, and understanding of what my life is for?
questions.christ_example: Christ continually oriented Himself toward the Father (John 5:19; 6:38; 8:29; 17:4). We orient ourselves toward Christ, who brings us to the Father.
questions.reflection_prompt: What part of my ordinary life is least consciously connected to Christ?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.5 - Is Jesus Christ increasingly the center of how I understand and live my life?"

anchors.1: Christ is important to me, but much of ordinary life is mentally and practically disconnected from Him.
anchors.4: I consciously look to Christ in many areas, but other parts of life remain largely separate.
anchors.7: Christ-centered living is increasingly characteristic: I look to Him as the center from which I understand relationships, decisions, difficulties, opportunities, weaknesses, priorities, hopes, and purpose.

questions.title: Does Jesus Christ naturally enter my everyday conversation?
questions.prompt: During the past several weeks, when appropriate, how naturally and sincerely did I speak of Jesus Christ, His teachings, His goodness, or what I am learning from Him rather than keeping discipleship almost entirely private?
questions.christ_example: Jesus openly testified of the Father and His mission throughout His ministry (John 8:28-29; 17:3-4).
questions.reflection_prompt: Would people who know me well know that Jesus Christ matters deeply to me?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.6 - Does Jesus Christ naturally enter my everyday conversation?"

anchors.1: I almost never speak of Christ outside formal Church settings.
anchors.4: I sometimes speak of Him when the setting clearly invites it, but I often hesitate.
anchors.7: Speaking naturally and appropriately of Christ is increasingly characteristic; He is sufficiently central to my life that references to Him arise sincerely rather than artificially.

questions.title: Do I surrender my will to God?
questions.prompt: When my desires conflict with what I believe God wants, how consistently do I sincerely seek to yield my will to His rather than asking Him merely to bless what I have already decided?
questions.christ_example: Jesus Christ's defining expression was, 'not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42).
questions.reflection_prompt: What decision or desire am I least willing to place before God without conditions?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.7 - Do I surrender my will to God?"

anchors.1: I generally protect my own will when obedience would require meaningful change.
anchors.4: I surrender in some areas but continue negotiating with God in others.
anchors.7: Yielding my will to God is increasingly characteristic; I seek His will without predetermining the answer and act upon what I believe He asks.

questions.title: Why do I obey?
questions.prompt: When I obey God, how much is my obedience increasingly motivated by love for Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ rather than primarily habit, fear, social expectation, guilt, duty, or anticipated blessings?
questions.christ_example: Christ obeyed the Father because He loved Him and always did what pleased Him (John 8:29; 14:31).
questions.reflection_prompt: If no one knew and no immediate blessing followed, would I still choose the same obedience?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.8 - Why do I obey?"

anchors.1: My obedience is mostly external or driven by fear, pressure, habit, or reward.
anchors.4: My motives are mixed; love is present but not consistently the dominant reason.
anchors.7: Love and trust in God increasingly animate my obedience, even when obedience is inconvenient or unseen.

questions.title: Do I put Christ first when priorities compete?
questions.prompt: When discipleship competes with comfort, convenience, reputation, entertainment, work, possessions, or other legitimate interests, how consistently does following Jesus Christ receive first claim on me?
questions.christ_example: Jesus taught that discipleship sometimes requires leaving lesser priorities to follow Him (Matthew 4:18-22; 19:21).
questions.reflection_prompt: What good thing most often competes successfully with what matters more?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.9 - Do I put Christ first when priorities compete?"

anchors.1: Other priorities routinely displace what I believe Christ asks of me.
anchors.4: Christ is first in principle, but competing priorities often win in practice.
anchors.7: Putting Christ first is increasingly characteristic; other good things are ordered beneath my discipleship rather than replacing it.

questions.title: Do I actively seek the Holy Ghost?
questions.prompt: During the past seven days, how intentionally did I seek the companionship, teaching, correction, comfort, and guidance of the Holy Ghost rather than assuming spiritual direction would come without effort?
questions.christ_example: Christ promised the Comforter to teach and guide His disciples (John 14:26; 16:13).
questions.reflection_prompt: What would I do differently today if receiving the Spirit's guidance were a conscious priority?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.10 - Do I actively seek the Holy Ghost?"

anchors.1: I give little deliberate attention to seeking the Holy Ghost.
anchors.4: I seek the Spirit in obvious spiritual settings or difficult decisions but inconsistently in ordinary life.
anchors.7: Seeking the Holy Ghost is increasingly characteristic; I pray, listen, study, worship, and make choices with a real desire to receive divine guidance.

questions.title: Do I act on spiritual promptings?
questions.prompt: Think of recent impressions you reasonably believed may have come from the Holy Ghost. How consistently did you seek appropriate confirmation when needed and then act rather than postponing, dismissing, or rationalizing the prompting away?
questions.christ_example: Jesus acted in perfect harmony with the Father and Spirit, doing what the Father showed Him (John 5:19).
questions.reflection_prompt: What prompting have I delayed that may still require action?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.11 - Do I act on spiritual promptings?"

anchors.1: I frequently ignore or postpone impressions I believe may be from the Spirit.
anchors.4: I act on some promptings but hesitate when they are inconvenient, uncertain, or uncomfortable.
anchors.7: Responding to spiritual prompting is increasingly characteristic; I seek discernment and then act promptly and appropriately.

questions.title: Do I live in a way that invites the companionship of the Holy Ghost?
questions.prompt: How consistently do my choices, environments, media, speech, relationships, and private conduct invite rather than knowingly diminish the influence of the Holy Ghost?
questions.christ_example: Jesus was filled with and led by the Spirit (Luke 4:1, 14, 18).
questions.reflection_prompt: What recurring choice most affects my ability to recognize the Spirit?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "1.12 - Do I live in a way that invites the companionship of the Holy Ghost?"

anchors.1: I knowingly maintain patterns that frequently dull spiritual sensitivity.
anchors.4: I generally seek good influences but tolerate some choices I know make spiritual attentiveness harder.
anchors.7: Living to invite the Spirit is increasingly characteristic; when I recognize something diminishing His influence, I repent and adjust.

questions.title: How do I love people who can do nothing for me?
questions.prompt: Think of recent interactions with people from whom you had little to gain socially, professionally, financially, or personally. How consistently did you show genuine interest, dignity, kindness, and love?
questions.christ_example: Christ repeatedly gave attention to people with little social status or ability to repay Him (Luke 14:12-14; Mark 10:13-16).
questions.reflection_prompt: Who receives less of my love because I expect little from them?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.1 - How do I love people who can do nothing for me?"

anchors.1: My attention and warmth depend heavily on usefulness, status, similarity, or reciprocity.
anchors.4: I am generally courteous but invest more naturally where there is some benefit or connection.
anchors.7: Disinterested love is increasingly characteristic; I treat people as valuable children of God regardless of what they can do for me.

questions.title: What happens when another person's need interrupts my plans?
questions.prompt: Recall recent times when someone needed help, attention, listening, or compassion at an inconvenient moment. How did you respond?
questions.christ_example: Christ repeatedly allowed human need to interrupt planned movement or rest (Mark 5:21-34; 6:30-34).
questions.reflection_prompt: Do people experience my schedule as more important than they are?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.2 - What happens when another person's need interrupts my plans?"

anchors.1: I usually protect my plans and experience the person mainly as an interruption.
anchors.4: I sometimes adjust, but my willingness depends on convenience and urgency.
anchors.7: Compassion increasingly outranks convenience when appropriate; I discern responsibly and willingly make room for people.

questions.title: Do I notice people who are overlooked?
questions.prompt: During the past several weeks, how consistently did I notice and include people who were lonely, new, quiet, marginalized, grieving, awkward, elderly, young, or otherwise easy to pass by?
questions.christ_example: Christ noticed Zacchaeus, children, lepers, the blind, and others many people overlooked (Luke 19:1-10; Mark 10:46-52).
questions.reflection_prompt: Who around me may be nearly invisible to everyone else?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.3 - Do I notice people who are overlooked?"

anchors.1: I rarely notice unless someone draws attention to the need.
anchors.4: I sometimes notice and respond, especially when the need is obvious.
anchors.7: Seeing overlooked people is increasingly characteristic; I scan beyond my usual circle and act with inclusion and dignity.

questions.title: Does compassion move me to act?
questions.prompt: When I feel concern for another person, how consistently does that concern become appropriate action rather than remaining only a feeling or good intention?
questions.christ_example: Christ was 'moved with compassion' and then healed, taught, fed, or served (Matthew 14:14; Mark 6:34).
questions.reflection_prompt: What compassionate feeling have I not yet turned into appropriate action?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.4 - Does compassion move me to act?"

anchors.1: I often feel concern but rarely translate it into action.
anchors.4: I act when the need is clear or manageable but often stop at sympathy.
anchors.7: Compassion increasingly moves my hands as well as my heart; I seek appropriate ways to help.

questions.title: Can I genuinely rejoice in another person's good?
questions.prompt: Think of recent times someone else received recognition, success, opportunity, happiness, possessions, or blessings you might also desire. How sincerely did you rejoice?
questions.christ_example: Christ rejoiced in the faith and spiritual progress of others and directed glory to the Father (Luke 10:21).
questions.reflection_prompt: Whose success is hardest for me to celebrate, and why?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.5 - Can I genuinely rejoice in another person's good?"

anchors.1: Another person's good often triggers envy, comparison, resentment, or minimization.
anchors.4: I can congratulate others, though comparison or envy sometimes remains beneath the surface.
anchors.7: Rejoicing with others is increasingly characteristic; their good can genuinely increase my joy without diminishing my sense of worth.

questions.title: Do I love across meaningful differences?
questions.prompt: How consistently do I show sincere respect, kindness, curiosity, and goodwill toward people whose culture, beliefs, politics, personality, background, lifestyle, or opinions differ significantly from mine?
questions.christ_example: Christ crossed entrenched social and religious boundaries, including with the Samaritan woman (John 4:4-30).
questions.reflection_prompt: Which kind of person is easiest for me to treat as a category instead of a child of God?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.6 - Do I love across meaningful differences?"

anchors.1: Difference easily becomes distance, contempt, stereotyping, or dismissal.
anchors.4: I am respectful in many settings but more loving toward people who resemble or agree with me.
anchors.7: Love across difference is increasingly characteristic; disagreement does not erase dignity, curiosity, or goodwill.

questions.title: How do I love people who have hurt or opposed me?
questions.prompt: Think of people who have offended, rejected, criticized, mistreated, or opposed you. How consistently do you seek their good while maintaining any appropriate boundaries?
questions.christ_example: Christ prayed for those crucifying Him (Luke 23:34).
questions.reflection_prompt: Can I seek someone's good without pretending what they did was good?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.7 - How do I love people who have hurt or opposed me?"

anchors.1: I nurture hostility, contempt, retaliation, or a desire for their harm.
anchors.4: I avoid retaliation but struggle to desire their good or pray for them sincerely.
anchors.7: Christlike love toward opponents is increasingly characteristic; I seek their good, pray for them, and refuse hatred while maintaining wise boundaries.

questions.title: Do I try to see people as Christ sees them?
questions.prompt: When I encounter weakness, failure, difference, or difficult behavior in another person, how consistently do I remember their divine worth, complexity, potential, and need for grace rather than reducing them to a flaw or label?
questions.christ_example: Christ saw possibilities in imperfect disciples and called them forward (John 1:42; Luke 22:31-32).
questions.reflection_prompt: Whom have I reduced to a single story?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.8 - Do I try to see people as Christ sees them?"

anchors.1: I readily define people by faults, roles, labels, or what they have done to me.
anchors.4: I sometimes remember divine worth but still make quick, simplifying judgments.
anchors.7: Seeing whole persons is increasingly characteristic; I seek truth about behavior without losing sight of divine worth and potential.

questions.title: When I am with someone, am I truly present with them?
questions.prompt: When I am with another person, how consistently do I give that person genuine attention and presence rather than being physically present while my mind and attention are somewhere else?
questions.christ_example: Even while responding to Jairus's urgent need, Christ stopped and gave full attention to the woman who touched His garment (Mark 5:25-34).
questions.reflection_prompt: Who is the most important person right now? Perhaps, very often, it is the person God has placed in front of me.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "2.9 - When I am with someone, am I truly present with them?"

anchors.1: I am frequently distracted or preoccupied and give people only partial attention.
anchors.4: I listen adequately when something is important, but ordinary interactions are often divided by devices, work, or my own thoughts.
anchors.7: Christlike presence is increasingly characteristic: I seek to truly see, hear, and understand the person before me and willingly set aside unnecessary distractions.

questions.title: How do I respond to correction?
questions.prompt: Think of the last three times someone corrected, challenged, or redirected you. How willing were you to listen, consider truth, and change?
questions.christ_example: Christ was sinless, yet modeled meekness and submission to the Father (John 5:30; Luke 22:42).
questions.reflection_prompt: When corrected, is my first goal to learn or to defend myself?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.1 - How do I respond to correction?"

anchors.1: I become defensive, dismissive, argumentative, or preoccupied with proving the correction wrong.
anchors.4: I can receive correction when it is clearly valid or respectfully delivered, but defensiveness remains common.
anchors.7: Teachability is increasingly characteristic; I listen for truth, ask what I can learn, and change when correction is warranted.

questions.title: Can I learn from criticism that is poorly delivered?
questions.prompt: When criticism is unfair, exaggerated, insensitive, or badly expressed, how consistently can I separate the manner of delivery from any truth I may still need to hear?
questions.christ_example: Christ endured unjust accusation without allowing others' conduct to determine His own (1 Peter 2:23).
questions.reflection_prompt: Am I using another person's imperfection to avoid examining my own?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.2 - Can I learn from criticism that is poorly delivered?"

anchors.1: Poor delivery becomes my reason to reject the message entirely.
anchors.4: I can sometimes find truth after my emotions settle, but I often focus first on the critic's faults.
anchors.7: Meekness is increasingly characteristic; I can reject what is false while still humbly asking whether God wants me to learn something.

questions.title: How readily do I admit when I am wrong?
questions.prompt: When evidence, conscience, or the Spirit shows that I was wrong, how quickly and plainly do I acknowledge it without excuse, minimization, blame shifting, or qualification?
questions.christ_example: Christ taught honest confession and reconciliation rather than self-justification (Matthew 5:23-24; Luke 18:9-14).
questions.reflection_prompt: What would I need to admit if I were not trying to protect my image?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.3 - How readily do I admit when I am wrong?"

anchors.1: I resist admitting wrong and tend to explain why my behavior was understandable.
anchors.4: I admit clear mistakes but often soften responsibility or delay acknowledgment.
anchors.7: Owning error is increasingly characteristic; I can say 'I was wrong' plainly, repair harm, and change course.

questions.title: How much do I need recognition?
questions.prompt: When I do good work, serve, sacrifice, or contribute, how much does my satisfaction depend on being noticed, thanked, praised, credited, or seen as important?
questions.christ_example: Christ often withdrew from acclaim and directed glory to the Father (John 5:41; 8:50).
questions.reflection_prompt: Would I still do this good thing if nobody ever knew?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.4 - How much do I need recognition?"

anchors.1: I strongly need recognition and feel resentful or diminished when it does not come.
anchors.4: I can serve quietly in some areas but still care considerably about credit or appreciation.
anchors.7: Quiet service is increasingly characteristic; being known by God matters more than being noticed by others.

questions.title: Do I recognize my dependence upon God?
questions.prompt: In success, decision-making, spiritual growth, work, and ordinary life, how deeply do I recognize that I need God rather than treating Him as an optional addition to my own competence?
questions.christ_example: Christ declared His complete dependence upon and unity with the Father (John 5:19, 30).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where has competence quietly become self-sufficiency?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.5 - Do I recognize my dependence upon God?"

anchors.1: I function largely as though my abilities and plans are sufficient.
anchors.4: I acknowledge dependence on God in principle but often live self-sufficiently in practice.
anchors.7: Dependence upon God is increasingly characteristic; gratitude, prayer, humility, and seeking His will accompany both weakness and strength.

questions.title: What happens to my heart when I succeed?
questions.prompt: When I experience success, influence, wealth, recognition, spiritual progress, or unusual ability, how consistently do I remain grateful, teachable, generous, and aware of my dependence upon God?
questions.christ_example: Christ possessed all power yet used it to serve and glorify the Father (John 13:3-5; 17:4).
questions.reflection_prompt: What blessing is most likely to make me forget the Giver?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.6 - What happens to my heart when I succeed?"

anchors.1: Success tends to increase pride, entitlement, comparison, or self-importance.
anchors.4: I am grateful but sometimes begin to feel superior, self-sufficient, or deserving.
anchors.7: Success increasingly deepens gratitude and stewardship rather than pride; I remember the source of my blessings and use them for good.

questions.title: Can I be taught by someone I could consider beneath me?
questions.prompt: How willing am I to learn truth from someone younger, less educated, less experienced, lower in status, different from me, or otherwise easy for me to discount?
questions.christ_example: Christ received children and held them up as examples to adults (Mark 10:13-16).
questions.reflection_prompt: Whose voice do I discount before I have really listened?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.7 - Can I be taught by someone I could consider beneath me?"

anchors.1: Status or my judgment of the messenger often determines whether I listen.
anchors.4: I can learn from unexpected people when their expertise is obvious, but pride sometimes interferes.
anchors.7: Humility is increasingly characteristic; I care more about truth than the status of the person through whom it comes.

questions.title: Do I sincerely seek truth, help, counsel, and correction?
questions.prompt: When I do not know, understand, or know what to do, how willing am I to seek truth by sincerely asking God and appropriate trusted people for help, counsel, perspective, or correction - even when asking makes me feel vulnerable or risks embarrassment, disagreement, judgment, or discovering that I may be wrong?
questions.christ_example: Christ taught His disciples to ask, seek, and knock (Matthew 7:7-8).
questions.reflection_prompt: Whom should I ask, 'What am I not seeing?'
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "3.8 - Do I sincerely seek truth, help, counsel, and correction?"

anchors.1: I avoid asking when doing so could expose weakness or challenge my preferred view.
anchors.4: I seek help in some areas but tend to ask people who will confirm what I already think.
anchors.7: Seeking truth is increasingly characteristic; I ask God and appropriate people sincerely and remain willing to be corrected.

questions.title: Who am I when no one will know?
questions.prompt: Think about choices you make when discovery, praise, embarrassment, or social consequences are unlikely. How consistently do your private choices match what you believe is right?
questions.christ_example: Christ's private and public devotion were one; He sought the Father's will even alone (Mark 1:35).
questions.reflection_prompt: What choice would change if I knew it would become public tomorrow?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.1 - Who am I when no one will know?"

anchors.1: My private behavior differs materially from the standards I present publicly.
anchors.4: I am generally consistent but make exceptions when I believe there will be no consequences.
anchors.7: Integrity is increasingly characteristic; unseen choices are governed by conscience and discipleship, not by whether anyone will know.

questions.title: Is my private self consistent with my public presentation?
questions.prompt: How closely do the person I present at church, work, online, and in public match the person my family and God see in private?
questions.christ_example: Christ condemned hypocrisy and taught inward righteousness (Matthew 23:25-28).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where am I managing an image instead of becoming the person the image suggests?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.2 - Is my private self consistent with my public presentation?"

anchors.1: I maintain a significant gap between public image and private character.
anchors.4: Most of my life is consistent, but I manage impressions or conceal meaningful contradictions.
anchors.7: Wholeness is increasingly characteristic; the same core values govern public and private life.

questions.title: Am I honest when honesty costs me?
questions.prompt: When truth threatens money, reputation, comfort, advantage, relationships, or embarrassment, how consistently do I tell the truth and deal fairly?
questions.christ_example: Christ testified of truth even when doing so contributed to His condemnation (John 18:37).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where does honesty currently cost me something?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.3 - Am I honest when honesty costs me?"

anchors.1: I shade, omit, distort, or conceal truth when the cost feels high enough.
anchors.4: I am usually honest but sometimes rationalize misleading omissions or convenient ambiguity.
anchors.7: Truthfulness is increasingly characteristic even when costly; I would rather lose an advantage than obtain it dishonestly.

questions.title: Can my word be trusted?
questions.prompt: How reliably do I keep promises, commitments, appointments, agreements, and representations I make to other people?
questions.christ_example: Jesus Christ is described as faithful and true (Revelation 19:11).
questions.reflection_prompt: Which commitment have I treated more casually than I would want others to treat a commitment to me?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.4 - Can my word be trusted?"

anchors.1: I frequently overpromise, forget, evade, or treat commitments casually.
anchors.4: I am generally dependable but make commitments too easily or fail to communicate promptly when I cannot fulfill them.
anchors.7: Trustworthiness is increasingly characteristic; my yes and no carry weight because I act consistently and communicate honestly.

questions.title: Do I rationalize behavior I suspect is wrong?
questions.prompt: When I feel spiritual discomfort about a choice, how consistently do I investigate honestly rather than constructing reasons that make the desired behavior seem acceptable?
questions.christ_example: Christ rejected Satan's attempts to misuse scripture to justify wrong action (Matthew 4:1-11).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where am I asking 'Can I get away with this?' instead of 'Is this pleasing to God?'
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.5 - Do I rationalize behavior I suspect is wrong?"

anchors.1: I often search for loopholes, comparisons, technicalities, or excuses that permit what I want.
anchors.4: I sometimes recognize rationalization after the fact but still use it in areas of strong desire.
anchors.7: Moral honesty is increasingly characteristic; discomfort leads me to seek truth and repent rather than to manufacture permission.

questions.title: What do I willingly allow to occupy my mind?
questions.prompt: How consistently did I seek cleanliness and virtue in my thoughts and in what I voluntarily allowed into my mind - and turn away from thoughts, entertainment, images, conversations, or other influences I recognized as lustful, degrading, cruel, vulgar, spiritually numbing, or otherwise inconsistent with following Jesus Christ?
questions.christ_example: Christ taught that righteousness reaches the heart and thoughts, not only outward acts (Matthew 5:27-28).
questions.reflection_prompt: What am I voluntarily feeding my mind?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.6 - What do I willingly allow to occupy my mind?"

anchors.1: I willingly consume or dwell on influences I know pull my mind away from virtue.
anchors.4: I avoid obvious extremes but make repeated compromises or linger longer than I believe is wise.
anchors.7: Purity of mind is increasingly characteristic; I choose influences deliberately and turn away when I recognize something degrading or spiritually numbing.

questions.title: What do I do with unrighteous desires?
questions.prompt: When an unrighteous desire, temptation, intrusive thought, or attraction arises, how consistently do I refuse to cultivate it and instead redirect my attention and choices toward what is good?
questions.christ_example: Christ experienced temptation yet remained without sin (Hebrews 4:15; Matthew 4:1-11).
questions.reflection_prompt: The question is not what entered my mind uninvited, but what I chose to do next.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.7 - What do I do with unrighteous desires?"

anchors.1: I voluntarily entertain or cultivate desires I recognize as inconsistent with discipleship.
anchors.4: I resist some desires but sometimes linger, fantasize, or feed them before redirecting.
anchors.7: Self-governance is increasingly characteristic; involuntary experiences are not treated as sin, but I choose not to cultivate what I believe is unrighteous.

questions.title: When I do wrong, do I own it honestly?
questions.prompt: When I recognize wrongdoing, how consistently do I name it honestly, confess where appropriate, make restitution or repair, and change rather than minimizing or hiding it?
questions.christ_example: Christ's parable of the publican commends honest acknowledgment before God rather than self-justification (Luke 18:13-14).
questions.reflection_prompt: What do I already know I need to repair?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "4.8 - When I do wrong, do I own it honestly?"

anchors.1: I conceal, minimize, blame, or wait for exposure before taking responsibility.
anchors.4: I usually acknowledge wrongdoing but may delay repair or soften responsibility.
anchors.7: Repentant integrity is increasingly characteristic; I bring wrong into the light, repair what I can, and change direction.

questions.title: How easily am I irritated?
questions.prompt: During the past week, how frequently did small delays, mistakes, inconveniences, noises, interruptions, or unmet expectations disturb my disposition?
questions.christ_example: Christ remained patient with slow-learning disciples (Mark 8:17-21).
questions.reflection_prompt: Which recurring irritation reveals the most about my present patience?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.1 - How easily am I irritated?"

anchors.1: Minor frustrations regularly control my mood or speech.
anchors.4: I manage some irritations well but still become noticeably impatient in recurring situations.
anchors.7: Patience is increasingly characteristic; ordinary annoyances rarely determine how I treat people or carry myself.

questions.title: How do I treat people who test my patience?
questions.prompt: Think of people who are slow, repetitive, difficult, demanding, disorganized, immature, or otherwise taxing for you. How consistently do you preserve dignity and kindness?
questions.christ_example: Christ repeatedly taught and corrected His disciples without abandoning them (Matthew 17:17-20; John 21:15-17).
questions.reflection_prompt: Who receives the least patient version of me?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.2 - How do I treat people who test my patience?"

anchors.1: My impatience becomes visible through tone, contempt, avoidance, sarcasm, or harshness.
anchors.4: I usually remain civil but my frustration often leaks into how I respond.
anchors.7: Patient love is increasingly characteristic; I can set limits or correct problems without treating the person as the problem.

questions.title: What do I do when anger arises?
questions.prompt: When you feel anger, how consistently do you govern what you say and do, seek understanding, and avoid retaliation, cruelty, intimidation, or unnecessary escalation?
questions.christ_example: Christ could confront wrongdoing forcefully without becoming governed by personal spite (Mark 3:5; John 2:13-17).
questions.reflection_prompt: When I say 'I was angry,' am I treating emotion as an explanation or an excuse?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.3 - What do I do when anger arises?"

anchors.1: Anger regularly controls my words or actions.
anchors.4: I often restrain outward behavior but still rehearse resentment or react sharply.
anchors.7: Righteous self-government is increasingly characteristic; I pause, discern what requires action, and respond without surrendering control to anger.

questions.title: Do I govern my appetites, impulses, and habits - or do they govern me?
questions.prompt: Consider food, spending, media, sex, substances, work, exercise, entertainment, technology, and other appetites or habits. How consistently are they governed by deliberate discipleship?
questions.christ_example: Christ fasted, resisted temptation, and governed bodily appetite in service of His mission (Matthew 4:1-4).
questions.reflection_prompt: Which appetite most often makes decisions for me?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.4 - Do I govern my appetites, impulses, and habits - or do they govern me?"

anchors.1: One or more appetites or habits regularly override my better judgment.
anchors.4: I exercise meaningful control but remain inconsistent in recurring areas.
anchors.7: Temperance is increasingly characteristic; appetites remain servants rather than masters, and I seek help when a pattern exceeds my ability to manage alone.

questions.title: Can I pause before reacting?
questions.prompt: When a strong emotion or impulse arises, how consistently can I create enough space to choose my response rather than simply following the first reaction?
questions.christ_example: When provoked or accused, Christ often responded deliberately rather than reflexively (John 8:3-11; Matthew 27:12-14).
questions.reflection_prompt: What practice would help me lengthen the space between feeling and choosing?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.5 - Can I pause before reacting?"

anchors.1: My first reaction often becomes my action.
anchors.4: I sometimes pause, but strong emotion or urgency frequently shortens the gap between impulse and response.
anchors.7: Deliberate response is increasingly characteristic: I habitually pause, consider consequences, seek perspective or the Spirit when appropriate, and intentionally choose what I believe is right.

questions.title: How do I respond when I have to wait?
questions.prompt: When people, traffic, lines, processes, answers, healing, progress, or desired outcomes take longer than I want, how consistently do I remain patient and constructive?
questions.christ_example: Christ sometimes deliberately waited for the Father's timing (John 7:6; 11:6).
questions.reflection_prompt: What does waiting reveal about what I believe I am entitled to?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.6 - How do I respond when I have to wait?"

anchors.1: Waiting commonly produces agitation, entitlement, complaint, or impulsive attempts to force outcomes.
anchors.4: I tolerate waiting but often become restless or negative.
anchors.7: Patient endurance is increasingly characteristic; I use waiting well and resist letting delay corrupt my disposition.

questions.title: How much do circumstances control my disposition?
questions.prompt: When plans fail, weather changes, people disappoint me, work becomes difficult, or comfort decreases, how much does my kindness, gratitude, and steadiness depend on circumstances going my way?
questions.christ_example: Christ maintained love and purpose amid rejection, fatigue, and suffering (Luke 9:51-56; John 19:26-27).
questions.reflection_prompt: Which circumstance has too much power over the person I become?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.7 - How much do circumstances control my disposition?"

anchors.1: My disposition rises and falls sharply with circumstances.
anchors.4: I remain steady in many situations but recurring conditions reliably alter how I treat others.
anchors.7: Inner steadiness is increasingly characteristic; circumstances affect me but do not dictate my character.

questions.title: Can I deny something good for a higher good?
questions.prompt: How willing am I to postpone or forego legitimate pleasures, opportunities, comfort, recognition, or convenience when a higher spiritual, family, service, or stewardship priority calls for it?
questions.christ_example: Christ repeatedly set aside comfort and rest to fulfill the Father's work (John 4:34; Mark 6:31-34).
questions.reflection_prompt: What good thing may currently be crowding out something better?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "5.8 - Can I deny something good for a higher good?"

anchors.1: If something is permissible and desirable, I rarely surrender it for a higher good.
anchors.4: I make some sacrifices but often choose immediate good over greater good.
anchors.7: Ordered desire is increasingly characteristic; I can willingly say no to a good thing when discipleship points to something better.

questions.title: How long do I hold resentment after I am hurt?
questions.prompt: Think of recent offenses or disappointments. How long did you continue rehearsing the injury, feeding resentment, or emotionally punishing the person?
questions.christ_example: Christ forgave amid extreme injury (Luke 23:34).
questions.reflection_prompt: What hurt am I keeping alive by repeatedly rehearsing it?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.1 - How long do I hold resentment after I am hurt?"

anchors.1: I hold resentment for long periods and repeatedly revisit the injury.
anchors.4: I eventually release many offenses but often after substantial rumination or emotional distance.
anchors.7: Forgiveness increasingly begins early; I acknowledge pain honestly while resisting the cultivation of resentment.

questions.title: Does my forgiveness depend on an apology?
questions.prompt: When someone has wronged you, how much does your willingness to release hatred and vengeance depend on that person apologizing, understanding, or repairing the harm first?
questions.christ_example: Christ extended forgiveness toward people who had not yet repaired the harm (Luke 23:34).
questions.reflection_prompt: Am I giving another person's repentance control over the condition of my heart?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.2 - Does my forgiveness depend on an apology?"

anchors.1: I withhold forgiveness until the other person does what I believe they owe me.
anchors.4: I know I should forgive, but my heart remains contingent on their response.
anchors.7: Forgiveness is increasingly characteristic even without apology; I stop requiring the other person to repair my heart first, while preserving wise boundaries and accountability.

questions.title: Do I take satisfaction when someone who hurt me suffers?
questions.prompt: When a person who offended or opposed you experiences embarrassment, loss, failure, or consequences, what happens in your heart?
questions.christ_example: Christ wept over Jerusalem even while foretelling consequences (Luke 19:41-44).
questions.reflection_prompt: Can I desire justice without needing another person's misery?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.3 - Do I take satisfaction when someone who hurt me suffers?"

anchors.1: I feel vindicated or pleased by their suffering and may want more of it.
anchors.4: I do not seek revenge but sometimes enjoy seeing them brought down.
anchors.7: Mercy is increasingly characteristic; I can support just consequences without delighting in another person's pain.

questions.title: Can I distinguish forgiveness from trust?
questions.prompt: When someone has caused harm, how wisely do I forgive while making separate, truthful decisions about trust, access, boundaries, safety, and consequences?
questions.christ_example: Christ loved all people but did not entrust Himself indiscriminately to everyone (John 2:24-25).
questions.reflection_prompt: What would forgiveness look like here if I stopped confusing it with access or trust?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.4 - Can I distinguish forgiveness from trust?"

anchors.1: I either confuse forgiveness with immediate trust or use boundaries as a reason to keep hatred alive.
anchors.4: I understand the distinction intellectually but apply it inconsistently.
anchors.7: Merciful wisdom is increasingly characteristic; I release vengeance while allowing trust to be rebuilt appropriately and maintaining necessary boundaries.

questions.title: Do I give people the benefit of a charitable interpretation?
questions.prompt: When another person's motives are unclear, how consistently do I resist assuming the worst and consider reasonable, charitable explanations while remaining honest about facts?
questions.christ_example: Christ often saw beyond surface behavior to deeper need and possibility (Luke 7:36-50).
questions.reflection_prompt: What story am I telling myself about someone's motives that I do not actually know?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.5 - Do I give people the benefit of a charitable interpretation?"

anchors.1: I quickly infer selfish, hostile, incompetent, or dishonest motives.
anchors.4: I sometimes suspend judgment but often settle on negative explanations without enough evidence.
anchors.7: Charitable interpretation is increasingly characteristic; I distinguish what I know from what I am assuming and remain open to a kinder truthful explanation.

questions.title: Am I gentle with other people's weaknesses?
questions.prompt: When someone is immature, struggling, repetitive, slow to change, or failing in an area where you are stronger, how consistently do you respond with patience and constructive help rather than contempt?
questions.christ_example: Christ dealt gently with imperfect disciples while continuing to call them upward (John 21:15-19).
questions.reflection_prompt: Which weakness in others is hardest for me to treat mercifully?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.6 - Am I gentle with other people's weaknesses?"

anchors.1: Weakness in others often produces superiority, irritation, ridicule, or dismissal.
anchors.4: I am compassionate in some areas but impatient with weaknesses I do not personally understand.
anchors.7: Gentleness is increasingly characteristic; I can hold standards while remembering my own dependence on grace.

questions.title: When I have power over consequences, do I lean toward mercy?
questions.prompt: When you have legitimate authority to punish, embarrass, exclude, penalize, or impose consequences, how consistently do you seek the most truthful and redemptive response rather than maximizing another person's pain?
questions.christ_example: Christ combined moral clarity with mercy toward the woman taken in adultery (John 8:3-11).
questions.reflection_prompt: Am I trying to correct the wrong, or make the person hurt?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.7 - When I have power over consequences, do I lean toward mercy?"

anchors.1: Power tends to make me punitive, retaliatory, or eager to make an example of someone.
anchors.4: I consider mercy but sometimes use more force or humiliation than the situation requires.
anchors.7: Merciful justice is increasingly characteristic; I uphold necessary consequences while seeking restoration, dignity, and the person's good.

questions.title: Can I remain compassionate when someone's own choices contributed to their suffering?
questions.prompt: When another person's poor decisions helped create their need, how consistently do I resist using blame as an excuse to harden my heart and instead discern what appropriate compassion requires?
questions.christ_example: The father of the prodigal son did not deny the son's choices, yet met his return with compassion (Luke 15:20-24).
questions.reflection_prompt: Am I using another person's responsibility as permission to stop loving?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "6.8 - Can I remain compassionate when someone's own choices contributed to their suffering?"

anchors.1: I readily conclude that people caused their problem and therefore deserve little concern from me.
anchors.4: I feel compassion but often withdraw help when I disapprove of how the need arose.
anchors.7: Compassion is increasingly characteristic; personal responsibility matters, but I do not use it to excuse indifference and I seek wise ways to help.

questions.title: What do I do when someone who is not present is criticized?
questions.prompt: When someone who isn't present is criticized, how consistently do I avoid unnecessarily adding to the criticism and, when appropriate, respond in a way that moves the conversation toward greater truth, fairness, compassion, or something constructive?
questions.christ_example: Christ defended people from demeaning judgment while still addressing truth (John 8:3-11).
questions.reflection_prompt: Did my contribution make the conversation more truthful and charitable?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.1 - What do I do when someone who is not present is criticized?"

anchors.1: I readily join criticism, gossip, ridicule, or speculation.
anchors.4: I usually avoid adding much but often remain passive when a constructive response would be appropriate.
anchors.7: Protecting others' dignity is increasingly characteristic; I seek the Spirit to discern whether to remain silent, redirect, clarify, defend, appropriately address a legitimate concern, or take another constructive action.

questions.title: Do I talk about people instead of talking to them?
questions.prompt: When I have a meaningful concern with someone, how consistently do I address it appropriately with the person or responsible party rather than repeatedly discussing it with uninvolved people?
questions.christ_example: Christ addressed people directly and truthfully (Matthew 16:23; John 4:17-18).
questions.reflection_prompt: Who do I need to speak with rather than continue speaking about?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.2 - Do I talk about people instead of talking to them?"

anchors.1: I commonly vent, recruit allies, or discuss problems around the person instead of with them.
anchors.4: I sometimes address issues directly but often process them with more people than necessary.
anchors.7: Appropriate directness is increasingly characteristic; I seek wise counsel when needed but resist triangulation and unnecessary gossip.

questions.title: Do I listen to understand - or listen to answer?
questions.prompt: During disagreement or emotionally important conversation, how consistently do I sincerely try to understand what the other person believes and the experiences, concerns, needs, and reasoning behind it?
questions.christ_example: Christ asked questions and drew people out before teaching them (Luke 24:17-27; John 5:6).
questions.reflection_prompt: Understanding does not require agreement.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.3 - Do I listen to understand - or listen to answer?"

anchors.1: I mainly listen for openings to rebut, correct, or defend myself.
anchors.4: I understand the words but often prepare my response before I have understood the person.
anchors.7: Listening to understand is increasingly characteristic; I listen with enough humility that I am willing to learn something even when I continue to disagree.

questions.title: Can I disagree strongly without diminishing the person?
questions.prompt: When I believe another person is seriously wrong, how consistently can I speak truthfully and firmly without contempt, ridicule, dehumanization, hostility, or treating disagreement as evidence that the person is my enemy?
questions.christ_example: Christ could speak hard truth while still loving the person before Him (Mark 10:21).
questions.reflection_prompt: Can I oppose an idea without needing to diminish the person who holds it?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.4 - Can I disagree strongly without diminishing the person?"

anchors.1: Strong disagreement readily becomes contempt or personal attack.
anchors.4: I remain civil but sometimes caricature motives, intelligence, or character.
anchors.7: Christlike disagreement is increasingly characteristic; I hold firmly to truth while seeking to understand and preserving the other person's dignity and worth.

questions.title: What do my words do to people?
questions.prompt: Looking at recent conversations, texts, emails, and online communication, how consistently do my words build, clarify, encourage, correct appropriately, and communicate truth with love rather than wound unnecessarily?
questions.christ_example: People marveled at Christ's gracious words even when His teaching was demanding (Luke 4:22).
questions.reflection_prompt: After people interact with me, what do my words leave behind?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.5 - What do my words do to people?"

anchors.1: My words frequently shame, belittle, inflame, gossip, manipulate, or injure.
anchors.4: My communication is usually acceptable but becomes sharp, careless, or unkind under stress.
anchors.7: Edifying speech is increasingly characteristic; even necessary correction is aimed at truth, dignity, and good.

questions.title: When conflict occurs, do I seek reconciliation and appropriate common ground?
questions.prompt: When meaningful conflict arises, how consistently do I seek to understand legitimate concerns, identify truthful areas of common ground, and work toward reconciliation or constructive solutions without surrendering principles I believe God requires?
questions.christ_example: Christ prayed for unity among His followers while preserving truth (John 17:20-23).
questions.reflection_prompt: Do I actually want peace and a good solution - or do I need to win?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.6 - When conflict occurs, do I seek reconciliation and appropriate common ground?"

anchors.1: I focus primarily on winning, vindication, or total acceptance of my position.
anchors.4: I want resolution but can become rigid, defensive, or unwilling to acknowledge legitimate concerns on the other side.
anchors.7: Peacemaking is increasingly characteristic; I seek understanding, appropriate common ground, and constructive resolution without unnecessary demands for total victory.

questions.title: Can I let an unnecessary argument go?
questions.prompt: When an issue is minor, unproductive, repetitive, or unlikely to benefit from continued debate, how consistently can I stop pressing my point rather than needing the last word?
questions.christ_example: Christ sometimes answered accusation and sometimes remained silent (Matthew 27:12-14).
questions.reflection_prompt: Is continuing this argument likely to produce any good?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.7 - Can I let an unnecessary argument go?"

anchors.1: I often continue until I feel heard, vindicated, or victorious.
anchors.4: I can disengage eventually but frequently spend too much energy proving a point.
anchors.7: Discernment is increasingly characteristic; I can distinguish truth worth defending from contention that should be released.

questions.title: Does my presence make relationships more peaceful?
questions.prompt: Across home, work, church, friendships, and groups, does my typical presence reduce unnecessary tension and increase truth, trust, patience, goodwill, and constructive cooperation?
questions.christ_example: Christ brought peace that was deeper than circumstance and invited His disciples to carry it (John 14:27).
questions.reflection_prompt: What atmosphere tends to follow me into a room?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.8 - Does my presence make relationships more peaceful?"

anchors.1: I often intensify tension, division, competition, or drama.
anchors.4: I generally avoid creating conflict but do not consistently help resolve or calm it.
anchors.7: Peacemaking influence is increasingly characteristic; people can often become more truthful, calm, and charitable because of how I participate.

questions.title: Am I becoming more like Jesus Christ in the way I love my family?
questions.prompt: In my relationships with family members, how consistently do I give them the love, attention, patience, forgiveness, service, respect, loyalty, and spiritual encouragement I seek to offer others - rather than allowing familiarity, busyness, work, personal interests, or accumulated frustrations to cause me to give those closest to me less of my best?
questions.christ_example: Christ honored family responsibilities and showed tender concern even from the cross (John 19:26-27).
questions.reflection_prompt: If my family were asked whether following Jesus Christ is making me more loving, present, patient, forgiving, dependable, and willing to serve at home, what would they say?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "7.9 - Am I becoming more like Jesus Christ in the way I love my family?"

anchors.1: Those closest to me often receive a less patient, attentive, respectful, or loving version of me than outsiders do.
anchors.4: I love my family deeply but consistency is mixed; busyness or familiarity often erodes my best intentions.
anchors.7: Christlike love at home is increasingly characteristic; those closest to me regularly experience my discipleship through presence, service, patience, loyalty, forgiveness, and spiritual encouragement.

questions.title: Am I faithful in the responsibilities God has entrusted to me?
questions.prompt: Consider family, church, work, community, promises, and other genuine stewardships. How consistently do I fulfill what is mine to do rather than neglecting it, procrastinating, or expecting others to carry it?
questions.christ_example: Christ completed the work the Father gave Him to do (John 17:4).
questions.reflection_prompt: What responsibility have I quietly stopped treating as sacred?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.1 - Am I faithful in the responsibilities God has entrusted to me?"

anchors.1: Important responsibilities are repeatedly neglected or left for others.
anchors.4: I am dependable in many areas but inconsistent where responsibility is difficult, boring, or unseen.
anchors.7: Faithfulness is increasingly characteristic; I can be trusted with what God and others legitimately place in my stewardship.

questions.title: Do I voluntarily look for opportunities to do good?
questions.prompt: Beyond assigned responsibilities, how consistently do I notice and initiate good that is mine to do rather than waiting to be asked?
questions.christ_example: Jesus 'went about doing good' rather than merely avoiding evil (Acts 10:38).
questions.reflection_prompt: What good could I reasonably do that no one has assigned me?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.2 - Do I voluntarily look for opportunities to do good?"

anchors.1: I mostly do good when it is assigned, requested, or convenient.
anchors.4: I sometimes initiate service but often wait for obvious invitations.
anchors.7: Proactive goodness is increasingly characteristic; I look for appropriate opportunities to bless, improve, encourage, repair, and serve.

questions.title: Once I recognize good or receive a prompting, do I act?
questions.prompt: Once I recognize something good that I believe I should do - or feel prompted by the Holy Ghost to do - how consistently do I actually act rather than allowing inconvenience, procrastination, uncertainty, discomfort, or distraction to leave the good undone?
questions.christ_example: Christ responded to needs with action, not merely sympathy (Mark 1:40-42).
questions.reflection_prompt: What good intention currently needs to become an action?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.3 - Once I recognize good or receive a prompting, do I act?"

anchors.1: Good intentions frequently remain intentions.
anchors.4: I act on many obvious needs but often delay when action is uncomfortable or inconvenient.
anchors.7: Acting upon recognized good is increasingly characteristic; I seek further guidance when needed and then act promptly and appropriately.

questions.title: Do I actively help others come unto Jesus Christ?
questions.prompt: When appropriate opportunities arise, how consistently do I act to help others come closer to Jesus Christ - by seeking those who may be spiritually lost or overlooked, living as His disciple, speaking naturally of Him, sharing testimony, inviting others to experience His gospel, serving, and following promptings about how I might help?
questions.christ_example: Christ described Himself as the shepherd who seeks the lost and repeatedly sought individuals others had overlooked (Luke 15:3-7; 19:10).
questions.reflection_prompt: We assess our willingness to seek, love, invite, testify, serve, and act - not another person's response.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.4 - Do I actively help others come unto Jesus Christ?"

anchors.1: I generally leave bringing others to Christ to someone else and rarely act on opportunities.
anchors.4: I sometimes invite, testify, or include others, but fear, busyness, or uncertainty often keeps me passive.
anchors.7: Helping others come to Christ is increasingly characteristic; I seek appropriate opportunities to love, invite, testify, teach, serve, include, and follow the Holy Ghost while respecting others' agency.

questions.title: Will I follow Christ when doing so costs me something?
questions.prompt: When following Christ threatens comfort, approval, money, opportunity, convenience, reputation, or another thing I value, how consistently do I choose discipleship?
questions.christ_example: Christ continued toward Jerusalem knowing the cost before Him (Luke 9:51).
questions.reflection_prompt: Courage is not the absence of fear. It is refusing to let fear make the final decision.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.5 - Will I follow Christ when doing so costs me something?"

anchors.1: Fear of cost commonly determines my choice.
anchors.4: I accept moderate costs but hesitate when sacrifice becomes personally significant.
anchors.7: Courageous discipleship is increasingly characteristic; fear may be present, but I refuse to let fear make the final decision.

questions.title: When hardship comes, do I continue turning toward Christ?
questions.prompt: During pain, disappointment, unanswered questions, loss, weakness, or prolonged difficulty, how consistently do I bring those experiences toward Christ rather than withdrawing from Him?
questions.christ_example: Christ turned toward the Father in the extremity of Gethsemane (Luke 22:41-44).
questions.reflection_prompt: Am I bringing my pain toward Christ or using it as a reason to move away?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.6 - When hardship comes, do I continue turning toward Christ?"

anchors.1: Hardship commonly makes me disengage spiritually, harden, or move away from Christ.
anchors.4: I continue many practices but sometimes distance myself emotionally or spiritually when relief is delayed.
anchors.7: Steadfastness in Christ is increasingly characteristic; hardship may deeply affect me, but I continue bringing pain, questions, weakness, and uncertainty toward Him.

questions.title: Can I faithfully wait upon the Lord?
questions.prompt: When God's answer or timing seems slow, uncertain, or different from what I want, how consistently do I seek His will and timeframe, continue doing the good that remains mine to do, and wait rather than forcing an outcome, giving up prematurely, or becoming spiritually disengaged?
questions.christ_example: Christ sometimes acted immediately and sometimes waited for the Father's timing (John 11:1-7).
questions.reflection_prompt: Sometimes faithfulness means acting courageously; sometimes continuing patiently; sometimes waiting without trying to force God's hand.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.7 - Can I faithfully wait upon the Lord?"

anchors.1: I tend to force outcomes, quit, or disengage when answers do not come on my timetable.
anchors.4: I wait in some areas but become impatient or controlling when the stakes are high.
anchors.7: Waiting upon the Lord is increasingly characteristic; I prayerfully seek His will and timeframe, do what He presently asks, remain attentive, and entrust outcomes to Him.

questions.title: Am I developing and using the gifts God has entrusted to me?
questions.prompt: How intentionally do I identify, develop, and use my abilities, opportunities, education, experience, influence, and spiritual gifts for good rather than burying them through fear, laziness, or self-absorption?
questions.christ_example: Christ's parable of the talents teaches accountable stewardship of entrusted capacity (Matthew 25:14-30).
questions.reflection_prompt: What gift am I burying that could bless someone?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "8.8 - Am I developing and using the gifts God has entrusted to me?"

anchors.1: I neglect significant gifts or use them primarily for myself.
anchors.4: I develop and use many abilities but leave some meaningful potential undeveloped or disconnected from service.
anchors.7: Stewardship of gifts is increasingly characteristic; I develop what God has entrusted to me and seek ways to multiply its good.

questions.title: Is my hope for the future anchored in Jesus Christ?
questions.prompt: When you think about your future, death, uncertainty, loss, or unresolved problems, how deeply is your hope rooted in Jesus Christ and His promises rather than favorable circumstances alone?
questions.christ_example: Christ taught resurrection and eternal life as grounds for hope amid death (John 11:25-26).
questions.reflection_prompt: What future outcome am I treating as necessary before I can have hope?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.1 - Is my hope for the future anchored in Jesus Christ?"

anchors.1: My hope depends heavily on circumstances turning out the way I want.
anchors.4: I believe in Christ but anxiety or pessimism often dominates my view of the future.
anchors.7: Hope in Christ is increasingly characteristic; uncertainty remains real, but it does not erase confidence in His goodness, Resurrection, grace, and promises.

questions.title: Do I deliberately notice and thank God for blessings?
questions.prompt: During the past seven days, how consistently did I consciously notice blessings and express specific gratitude to Heavenly Father rather than moving quickly past what is good?
questions.christ_example: Christ gave thanks to the Father even in ordinary acts such as blessing food (John 6:11; 11:41).
questions.reflection_prompt: What blessing have I become too accustomed to notice?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.2 - Do I deliberately notice and thank God for blessings?"

anchors.1: I rarely pause to notice or thank God unless something unusually good happens.
anchors.4: I express gratitude regularly but often mechanically or after being reminded.
anchors.7: Gratitude is increasingly characteristic; I deliberately notice ordinary and extraordinary gifts and thank God specifically.

questions.title: Can gratitude coexist with difficulty?
questions.prompt: When life is painful, disappointing, or uncertain, can I acknowledge the difficulty honestly while still recognizing genuine reasons for gratitude?
questions.christ_example: Christ gave thanks even in the shadow of suffering and loss (Matthew 26:26-28).
questions.reflection_prompt: Can I tell the truth about what hurts and still tell the truth about what is good?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.3 - Can gratitude coexist with difficulty?"

anchors.1: Difficulty tends to erase my awareness of blessing.
anchors.4: I can identify blessings intellectually but gratitude is fragile when pain is intense.
anchors.7: Mature gratitude is increasingly characteristic; sorrow and gratitude can coexist without either becoming dishonest.

questions.title: Do I allow Christ to help me grow through adversity?
questions.prompt: Without pretending suffering is itself good, how consistently do I bring weakness and adversity to Jesus Christ and allow His grace to deepen compassion, dependence, strength, wisdom, or Christlike character?
questions.christ_example: Because Christ suffered, He can succor us perfectly (Alma 7:11-12).
questions.reflection_prompt: Pain can enlarge our capacity to understand and succor someone else's pain.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.4 - Do I allow Christ to help me grow through adversity?"

anchors.1: Pain mostly hardens, narrows, or embitters me, and I rarely invite Christ into what it may teach.
anchors.4: I sometimes recognize growth after hardship but do not consistently seek redemptive transformation while in it.
anchors.7: Redemptive growth is increasingly characteristic; I bring adversity to Christ and allow His grace to transform what I experience.

questions.title: Do I receive and appropriately enjoy God's good gifts?
questions.prompt: How consistently do I recognize, receive, and appropriately enjoy the good things God has placed in my life rather than overlooking them, feeling unnecessary guilt for enjoying them, or being too focused on problems, responsibilities, or what comes next to experience joy now?
questions.christ_example: Christ attended meals, weddings, and gatherings and used created things with gratitude and purpose (John 2:1-11; Luke 7:34).
questions.reflection_prompt: What joy has God already placed in my life that I am failing to receive?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.5 - Do I receive and appropriately enjoy God's good gifts?"

anchors.1: I frequently overlook or cannot receive ordinary goodness and appropriate pleasure.
anchors.4: I enjoy many blessings but often rush past them or feel conflicted about receiving them.
anchors.7: Joyful receiving is increasingly characteristic; I receive appropriate pleasures gratefully and with judgment, not to excess, and let them deepen gratitude to God.

questions.title: Can I be content without having everything I desire?
questions.prompt: When something desirable remains unavailable, how consistently can I remain grateful and peaceful rather than making that thing a condition of happiness?
questions.christ_example: Christ lived without many worldly comforts while remaining centered on the Father's work (Matthew 8:20; John 4:34).
questions.reflection_prompt: What am I currently treating as a prerequisite for peace?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.6 - Can I be content without having everything I desire?"

anchors.1: I tend to believe I will be content once a desired circumstance, possession, relationship, or achievement arrives.
anchors.4: I can be content in many areas but recurring desires still exert too much control over my happiness.
anchors.7: Contentment is increasingly characteristic; I can desire something without requiring it for my happiness.

questions.title: What does comparison do to me?
questions.prompt: When you compare your appearance, success, wealth, family, gifts, spirituality, opportunities, or recognition with others, how consistently do you return to gratitude and your own discipleship rather than envy, superiority, or discouragement?
questions.christ_example: When Peter compared his future with John's, Christ answered, 'what is that to thee? follow thou me' (John 21:22).
questions.reflection_prompt: What is that to thee? Follow thou me.
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.7 - What does comparison do to me?"

anchors.1: Comparison frequently produces envy, pride, resentment, or diminished self-worth.
anchors.4: I recognize comparison as unhelpful but still spend significant mental energy on it.
anchors.7: Freedom from comparison is increasingly characteristic; I can appreciate others' paths and return attention to following Christ in my own stewardship.

questions.title: Can I experience peace before uncertainty is resolved?
questions.prompt: When important questions remain unanswered or outcomes remain unsettled, how consistently can I experience peace in Christ without requiring certainty first?
questions.christ_example: Christ offered peace to His disciples before their circumstances became easy (John 14:27; 16:33).
questions.reflection_prompt: What uncertainty am I trying to solve before I will permit myself peace?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.8 - Can I experience peace before uncertainty is resolved?"

anchors.1: I generally cannot be at peace until I know how things will turn out.
anchors.4: I experience periods of peace but repeatedly return to anxious attempts to control uncertainty.
anchors.7: Peace in Christ is increasingly characteristic; uncertainty remains, but I can entrust myself to Him without having every answer.

questions.title: Is following Jesus Christ becoming a source of joy?
questions.prompt: How much does discipleship itself - knowing Christ, worshipping, repenting, serving, obeying, learning, and feeling His grace - increasingly produce genuine joy rather than feeling primarily like obligation?
questions.christ_example: Christ taught so that His joy might remain in His disciples and their joy might be full (John 15:11).
questions.reflection_prompt: Where have I experienced the joy of actually following Christ?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.9 - Is following Jesus Christ becoming a source of joy?"

anchors.1: Discipleship feels mostly burdensome, external, or joyless.
anchors.4: I experience meaningful spiritual joy but inconsistently.
anchors.7: Joy in Christ is increasingly characteristic; following Him gives depth, meaning, gratitude, and gladness even when discipleship is demanding.

questions.title: Does the way I live help other people experience greater joy?
questions.prompt: Without pretending life is always easy or avoiding necessary truth, how intentionally do I help others recognize goodness, feel loved and valued, celebrate appropriate blessings, experience hope, enjoy life, and find deeper joy in Jesus Christ?
questions.christ_example: Christ blessed children, comforted mourners, healed suffering, and invited people into His joy (3 Nephi 17).
questions.reflection_prompt: Whose life could contain greater joy because of the way I choose to live?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "9.10 - Does the way I live help other people experience greater joy?"

anchors.1: My presence commonly adds heaviness, negativity, criticism, or discouragement.
anchors.4: I am supportive but do not consistently create or notice opportunities to increase wholesome joy.
anchors.7: Christlike joy increasingly flows outward through me; I help people experience hope, belonging, gratitude, appropriate delight, and deeper joy in Christ.

questions.title: What do I do when a need is directly in my path?
questions.prompt: When a meaningful need appears directly before me, how consistently do I respond with compassion and appropriate help rather than treating the person mainly as a problem or inconvenience?
questions.christ_example: The good Samaritan interrupted his journey and used his resources for the wounded man (Luke 10:33-35).
questions.reflection_prompt: When need interrupts me, do I see a person or merely a problem?
questions.source_locator: docx heading: "10.1 - What do I do when a need is directly in my path?"

anchors.1: I often pass by needs I could reasonably help meet.
anchors.4: I help when the need is obvious and convenient but hesitate when it costs time, money, or comfort.
anchors.7: Responsive service is increasingly characteristic; I discern wisely and act when a need is reasonably mine to address.

questions.title: Do I notice needs before I am asked?
questions.prompt: How consistently do I pay enough attention to recognize practical, emotional, spiritual, financial, or relational needs without requiring people to ask explicitly?
questions.christ_example: Christ frequently perceived needs before people fully articulated them (John 5:6; Mark 2:5).
questions.reflection_prompt: Who may need help but be unlikely to ask?
